query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers, systematic compositional tuning that increases interfacial lattice distortion and disrupts short-range order (SRO) will induce a shift from primarily dislocation-mediated plasticity to a diffusion-assisted creep mechanism under sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coatings with alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy layers exhibiting inherent compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and established interfacial SRO.
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the interlayer composition (e.g., via magnetron sputtering parameters) to intentionally modulate interfacial lattice distortion and the degree of SRO.
generation.conditions: Sustained (creep) loading under controlled temperatures and stress levels that are high enough to activate time-dependent plasticity, while maintaining the nanoscale multilayer coating architecture.
generation.structural_mediator: Interfacial short-range order and lattice distortion at the boundaries between FCC and BCC layers.
generation.mechanism: At lower lattice distortions, pronounced SRO impedes dislocation motion, leading to a dislocation-mediated creep regime. With increased interfacial lattice distortion (via composition tuning), the SRO is progressively disrupted, facilitating atomic diffusion and shifting the dominant creep mechanism towards diffusion-assisted plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with enhanced interfacial lattice distortion (and reduced SRO) will exhibit higher creep strain rates and altered microstructural markers (e.g., reduced density of persistent dislocation networks and increased evidence of diffusion-driven deformation) compared to the baseline multilayer coating.
generation.baseline: Multilayer coatings produced with standard composition settings that maintain a relatively high degree of interfacial SRO and lower lattice distortion, resulting in dislocation-dominant creep.
generation.boundary: The observed shift in creep mechanism is expected only if the nanoscale multilayer structure is preserved and the applied loading conditions are sufficient to activate both dislocation and diffusion processes; extreme conditions that induce phase transformations or coating delamination would lie outside the valid regime of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds for the transition between the two mechanisms remain uncertain and may depend on subtle variations in alloy composition, processing conditions, and test parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FCC/BCC high-entropy multilayer samples with systematically varied interlayer compositions to modulate interfacial lattice distortion and SRO. Subject these samples to sustained creep tests under controlled temperature and stress conditions while ensuring the multilayer architecture is maintained. Use in situ high-resolution microscopy (such as 4D-STEM) and post-mortem microstructural analysis to identify the dominant deformation mechanism (dislocation activity vs. diffusion evidence).
measurements: Creep strain rate as a function of time and applied stress
Density and character of dislocation networks through TEM/4D-STEM
Indicators of atomic diffusion (e.g., elemental redistribution or grain boundary changes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with increased interfacial lattice distortion show no significant shift in creep strain rate or microstructural markers—remaining predominantly dislocation-mediated despite the expected SRO disruption—or if diffusion-assisted mechanisms are observed equally in the baseline sample, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, nanoscale small-volume materials typically exhibit high strength but low tensile ductility. The latter is particularly important for the structural reliability of many micro/nanodevices. Here, we have achieved unusual room-temperature tensile ductility in excess of 100% under a high tensile flow stress in single-crystalline <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi HEA nanopillars. Our experimental, computational, and theoretical investigations showed that the ultrahigh uniform tensile ductility was caused by the intensive activation of distinct twinning mechanisms (nucleation, interaction, propagation, and coalescence of nanotwins) and extensive twin-dislocation interactions. These unique plasticity mechanisms originate from the atomic-level chemical complexity of the HEA that generates variable local SFEs and further synergistically coordinates a spatial activation of a series of deformation mechanisms. Our findings provide mechanistic insights for understanding plastic deformations of small-volume metallic materials and create a mechanistic map enabling the design of micro/nanodevices with reliable mechanical and functional properties. High or medium- entropy alloys (HEAs/MEAs) are multi-principal element alloys with equal atomic elemental composition, some of which have shown record-breaking mechanical performance. However, the link between short-range order (SRO) and the exceptional mechanical properties of these alloys has remained elusive. The local destruction of SRO by dislocation glide has been predicted to lead to a rejuvenated state with increased entropy and free energy, creating softer zones within the matrix and planar fault boundaries that enhance the ductility, but this has not been verified. Here, we integrate in situ nanomechanical testing with energy-filtered four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) and directly observe the rejuvenation during cyclic mechanical loading in single crystal CrCoNi at room temperature. Surprisingly, stacking faults (SFs) and twin boundaries (TBs) are reversible in initial cycles but become irreversible after a thousand cycles, indicating SF energy reduction and rejuvenation. AbstractIn aero-engine applications, turbine blades operate under high-temperature and high-pressure thermomechanical cyclic loading conditions, which demand exceptional mechanical performance. High-entropy superalloys, characterized by a stable dual-phase γ/γ′ microstructure, have emerged as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials due to their superior creep resistance. In this study, the creep behaviors of high-entropy superalloys are systematically investigated using molecular dynamics simulations, exploring the effects of stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction on creep deformation mechanisms. The results show that both stress and temperature significantly influence creep behavior, with temperature exerting a more dominant effect. As the applied stress increases, the dominant creep mechanism evolves from atomic diffusion to dislocation nucleation and motion, eventually leading to phase transformation. Additionally, the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction are found to critically affect the alloy’s creep resistance. As a salient feature pertaining to MPEAs, an intriguing question remains as to whether or how SRO affects the strongest size, maximum strength, and the underlying deformation mechanisms. Within the numerous MPEA systems, the face-centered cubic (fcc) CrCoNi-based alloys have attracted extensive attention owing to their extraordinary mechanical properties, including high strength and ductility (, ). The mechanistic origin of superior mechanical performance is traced to their low stacking faculty energy, which facilitates twining and phase transformation during mechanical straining. Twinning-induced plasticity and transformation-induced plasticity, known as TWIP and TRIP effects from advanced steels (), provide extra interface hardening and defer the onset of necking, contributing to an enhanced strength-ductility synergy. When the SRO is engineered into the materials, both stacking fault (SF) energy and activation energy barrier of dislocation motion are increased (), which likely alters the dislocation slip pathway and, hence, deformation microstructures (for instance, nanotwin and martensitic transformation). frame.goal: To elucidate the mechanistic origin of progressive plastic deformation (creep) under sustained loading while maintaining a balance between high strength and deformation tolerance.
frame.limitation: Conventional deformation frameworks from simpler metallic multilayers do not directly apply because preliminary evidence in high-entropy systems is insufficient to identify which creep mechanism dominates under varying conditions.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy alloys focused on identifying dislocation dynamics, phase transformation, and local lattice effects in relatively simple, bulk or single‐phase systems. Researchers first elucidated dislocation mechanisms and heterogeneous slip (e.g., PMC4949441) and then used atomistic simulations to reveal the impact of chemical clustering and short-range order on deformation (e.g., PMC4976365). Later work uncovered how stress‐induced phase transformations, amorphization, and rejuvenation of planar defects (PMC5893566, PMC7846165, PMC10873362) play roles under severe deformation, and most recently molecular dynamics simulations have addressed creep behavior specifically (PMC12842692). However, none of these studies directly addressed the role of interfacial short-range order and lattice distortion within the confined nanoscale multilayer architecture of FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coatings under sustained load.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved how the interplay between compositional complexity-induced lattice distortions and interfacial short-range order in FCC/BCC high-entropy multilayers controls the activation and dominance of distinct creep mechanisms under sustained loading. Specifically, the influence of tuned interlayer chemistry on the transition between dislocation-mediated progressive plasticity and diffusion-assisted creep is not yet isolated.
decision.lever: systematic composition tuning to modulate interfacial lattice distortion and short-range order
decision.why: Building on the trend that demonstrates how local SRO breakdown and lattice distortions govern deformation in HEAs—and noting that MD simulations have recently highlighted a stress- and temperature-driven transition in creep mechanisms—a controlled experiment in which the multilayer composition is systematically varied (using methods such as magnetron sputtering to ensure nanoscale layering) directly tests whether variations in interfacial SRO and lattice distortion drive the shift from dislocation-mediated plasticity to diffusion-assisted creep. This experiment fits the niche of probing the untested conditions in high-entropy systems and uses well‐established levers to expose the mechanistic origin of progressive deformation.
